summary: Explains that IP fragmentation can be used to disguise TCP packets from filters in routers and hosts. It describes two methods of attack and the remedies to prevent them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IP fragmentation can split a TCP header so a packet filter does not see the fields it is meant to check. This memo describes two fragment attacks and filtering rules intended to block them.

questions: how do ip fragments bypass firewalls
what is the tiny fragment attack
what is the overlapping fragment attack
how to block tiny fragment attacks
how can ip fragments bypass a packet filter
subtitle: How tiny and overlapping IP fragments can bypass packet filters, and how the memo proposes blocking them.

tldr.problem: A packet filter may inspect only the first IP fragment, allowing a sender to hide or change TCP header fields in later fragments.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes tiny-fragment and overlapping-fragment attacks and proposes dropping certain TCP fragments, including fragments with offset 1.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1858 is an Informational security memo. The unit metadata lists RFC 3128 as updating it.

today: RFC 1858 is an Informational memo published in October 1995 and was updated by RFC 3128. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Fragment Filtering Matters
sections.content:
Packet filters help administrators restrict traffic entering private networks. IP fragmentation can complicate filtering because a router often treats each fragment as part of a packet whose complete structure is hidden from the filter's user interface.

The memo explains that attackers can exploit how filters inspect fragments. It focuses on two methods: making the first fragment too small to contain important TCP fields, and using overlapping fragments to change header data after the filter has checked it.
sections.plainLanguage: A filter may inspect only some pieces of a fragmented packet. If important TCP fields are hidden in another piece, a packet that should be blocked may pass.

sections.title: How Filters Handle Fragments
sections.content:
One possible method stores the filter decision for the zero-offset fragment and applies that result to later fragments. It has weaknesses if fragments arrive out of order or take different paths through the network, because the filter may not see all fragments.

The memo describes the usual practice as filtering the first fragment and passing non-first fragments, on the assumption that the destination cannot reassemble a packet if the first fragment is missing. It also says pathological fragment sequences are not used in normal practice and can safely be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: A router may remember whether the first fragment passed and apply that decision to later pieces. Out-of-order fragments or multiple paths make that approach unreliable.

sections.title: Tiny Fragment Attack
sections.content:
A sender can make fragments unusually small. If the first fragment carries only the source and destination ports but places TCP flags in the next fragment, a filter that checks flags such as SYN and ACK cannot match them. The non-first fragment may pass without inspection.

RFC 791 requires an internet module to forward a datagram of 68 octets without further fragmentation, but the memo says that ensuring eight data octets in the first fragment is not enough for security because important transport fields may occur later. A direct defence compares the transport-header length in the first fragment with a filter-dependent minimum called TMIN and drops it if too short. The indirect method drops fragments with offset 1; that also prevents the destination from reassembling the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A tiny first fragment can hide TCP flags from a filter. The memo proposes checking that the first fragment is long enough or dropping the particular later fragment that would let the packet be reassembled.

sections.title: Overlapping Fragment Attack
sections.content:
The RFC describes an IP reassembly method where a new fragment overwrites data from an earlier fragment in an overlapping region. An attacker can put harmless TCP flags in the first fragment and different flags in an overlapping later fragment. The filter checks the first fragment, but a receiver may reconstruct a connection request from the later data.

The memo notes that receiver behavior for overlaps was not uniformly guaranteed. It proposes that a router enforce a minimum offset for non-zero-offset TCP fragments. In the described case, a TCP fragment with offset 1 begins only eight octets into the transport header, so the memo gives the general filter rule: if the offset is 1 and the protocol is TCP, drop the packet. The memo notes this might not suffice if a filter examines fields beyond the sixteenth octet of a transport header.
sections.plainLanguage: Overlapping fragments can replace TCP fields after the filter has checked them. Dropping TCP fragments with offset 1 blocks the examples described and also blocks the tiny-fragment method.

sections.title: Security Scope and Status
sections.content:
The memo's Security Considerations section says that the document is concerned entirely with security implications of filtering fragmented IP packets. It provides analysis and filtering approaches rather than specifying an Internet standard.

The unit metadata records RFC 3128 as an update to this memo. The discussion here describes the threats and remedies set out in RFC 1858's text.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is entirely about the security of filtering fragmented packets. The unit metadata identifies RFC 3128 as a later update.

viz.caption: RFC 1858'S GENERAL TCP FRAGMENT FILTER RULE

data.title: Drop offset-1 TCP fragments
data.code:
IF FO=1 and PROTOCOL=TCP then
        DROP PACKET
